I’ll review the material folder first, then shape a site concept and scroll-by-scroll plan around your work and personality.


The strongest direction is **“Closer to care”**: a portfolio about closing the distance between how clinical systems work and what nurses need in the moment.

Your material has a distinctive point of view: eleven years in nursing, experience leading shifts, and a habit of asking why the system makes the safe thing the slow thing. That should drive the visual experience. The 3D and movement should reveal those practical problems and the thinking behind your work.

I’d plan this primarily for clinical informatics hiring panels and potential collaborators, with enough clinical context that nursing colleagues recognise the work.

**The idea and first impression**

The site opens with your name, a clear professional description, and this proposed headline:

> **The safe thing should be the easy thing.**  
> I’m Aoife Brennan, a nurse and clinical informatics practitioner in Dublin. I improve the systems nurses use when every minute matters.

Beside it sits a restrained 3D scene: a schematic working surface with a handover sheet, a scanner dock, and a line connecting points of care. Warm paper, dark ink, subtle depth. It should feel tactile and precise.

The scene is illustrative, not a reconstruction of your ward. As the visitor scrolls, the distance between elements reduces and the information becomes clearer. That gives the movement a purpose rooted in your scanner research.

A small navigation stays available: **Work · About · Contact**, with a visible **View my work** link from the opening screen.

One factual correction matters before publication: LinkedIn says “Clinical Informatics Lead,” while your note gives the formal role as **Nursing Informatics Link Nurse, one day a week**. Use the formal title alongside **Clinical Nurse Manager 1**; describe the leadership through your actual contributions.

**What happens from top to bottom**

| Part | What it shows | What happens as you scroll |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Your point of view** | Name, role, headline and short introduction. A compact evidence line: **11 years nursing · Handover adopted on 6 wards · Scanning 71% → 94%**. | The 3D surface gently turns toward the reader. The text is readable immediately, with no loading sequence or animation gate. |
| **2. The conditions of the work** | A short passage about coordinating care on a 28-bed cardiac step-down ward. Your note about the night with nine admissions supplies a human opening. | The scene settles into a flat, readable composition. A recreated fragment of ward coordination could appear here once suitable material exists. |
| **3. Featured work: medication scanning** | The strongest documented case study: what nurses were working around, how you investigated it, what changed, and the result. | Three short stages bring the problems and interventions into view. A simple diagram shows the scanner moving closer to where it is needed. It stops moving when the reader reaches the evidence. |
| **4. Featured work: nursing handover** | Why the handover sheet needed changing, your role in the redesign, and adoption across six wards. | Old and new sheets appear in alignment, with annotations explaining verified changes. On desktop, an optional comparison control lets visitors inspect them. |
| **5. The wider practice** | Falls and pressure-ulcer audit dashboards, preceptorship of 14 newly qualified nurses, and your MSc studies. | A quieter editorial layout replaces the large scene. Small, optional reveals keep the rhythm without competing with the content. |
| **6. The person behind the work** | A short first-person account of how bedside nursing shaped your approach to informatics, followed by a compact career and education timeline. | Movement eases away. A natural portrait, if you want one, makes this the most personal part of the page. |
| **7. An invitation** | A clear contact route, LinkedIn and an accessible CV download. The closing line should reflect the opportunities you actually want. | A static, warm ending with no final animation to wait through. |

The homepage should tell a complete story in a few minutes. The two main projects should also have their own shareable pages for readers who want detail.

**How the work earns attention**

The medication-scanning case should lead. Its title could be **“Understanding why nurses skip the scan.”**

Build its narrative around the strongest line in the poster: **“None was laziness.”** Follow it with the evidence:

- Forty hours of observation and interviews with 22 nurses.
- Three recurring workarounds, each saving between one and four minutes per round.
- Changes to scanner placement, wristband stock and the use of printed barcodes.
- Scanning rising from **71% to 94% over nine months**.

Show that as a simple before-and-after comparison. There are no monthly measurements in the supplied material, so don’t invent a smooth trend chart. Describe the change as a **23 percentage-point increase in scanning**, without implying that a reduction in medication errors was measured.

Credit the 2025 conference poster and distinguish your contribution from the wider team’s implementation.

The handover project should provide a different kind of evidence: close reading of an actual tool. Once the old and new sheets are available, explain two or three specific design decisions. Six-ward adoption is already a useful result; claims about time saved or fewer omissions need additional evidence.

The audit dashboards currently have too little detail for full case studies. Give them concise supporting mentions until examples and context are available.

**Colour, type and visual character**

Use a warm, readable palette:

| Colour | Role |
|---|---|
| **Paper — `#F4F0E7`** | Main background and document surfaces |
| **Ink — `#172D32`** | Body text, navigation and strong contrast |
| **Deep teal — `#246A67`** | Links, active states and diagram emphasis |
| **Clay — `#B5684E`** | Small markers and decorative annotations |

Teal and clay should support labels and shapes, never carry meaning alone. Check contrast in the actual combinations before launch.

Pair **Source Serif 4** for large editorial headlines with **Source Sans 3** for body copy, captions and interface text. The serif gives your own words presence; the sans keeps the evidence straightforward to read. Use large margins, fine rules, numbered figure captions and selective oversized figures.

The imagery should come from your work: permission-cleared documents, recreated diagrams, and perhaps a portrait. Avoid generic hospital photography. Put the visual ambition into composition, depth and transitions.

**How it holds up on a phone**

The mobile version gets its own composition:

- Replace the live 3D scene with a carefully framed still or lightweight illustration.
- Keep the headline, role and first work link visible early.
- Stack the case-study stages in normal reading order.
- Present the handover sheets as labelled “Before” and “After” views with readable annotations; avoid a precision slider on a narrow screen.
- Keep all explanations available without hovering, dragging or watching animation.
- Use native scrolling throughout, with no scroll hijacking.

For reduced-motion preferences, show settled compositions and all content immediately. Keyboard navigation, visible focus, semantic headings, generous touch targets and accessible document downloads belong in the initial design.

**What else the site needs**

Before design moves into production, the missing material is quite specific:

- **Old and new handover sheets**, with enough explanation to establish what changed and what you personally did.
- **A safe way to represent the whiteboard.** Prefer a synthetic recreation with invented entries, clearly labelled. A real ward photograph can expose patient or staff information even after obvious names are removed.
- **Confirmation of your public title and MSc status.** The listed dates don’t establish whether the degree is complete.
- **Your preferred opportunities and contact details**, plus a current CV and optional portrait.
- **Permission for any employer-owned documents or imagery.** The site should clearly read as your personal portfolio.

Keep the identifiable medication near-miss details out of public copy; your motivation can be explained without a patient reference or bed number.

The build should eventually include fast, indexable project pages; page titles and social previews; an accessible CV; and a simple content structure you can update. Load any desktop 3D after the essential text, with a static fallback on slower devices. A direct email link is enough to start; a contact form adds maintenance and data-handling needs.

The site’s signature moment is the connection between the moving diagram and your finding: bringing a scanner closer to care helped make the safer action easier. That is a visual story specific to your work, with evidence to hold the visitor’s attention after the movement stops.

No site has been built or files changed.
